result.statement: To find the centre of a given circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle. Take any two points A, B on its circumference and join the straight line AB (P1).

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at the point D (1.10), so that AD = DB.

**Step 3.** From D draw DC at right angles to AB (1.11), C being the point in which this perpendicular meets the circumference; then the angles ADC, BDC are right (D1.10). Produce CD in a straight line beyond D to meet the circumference again at E (P2). Thus CE is a straight line through D, at right angles to AB, terminated at both ends by the circumference, with D lying between C and E.

**Step 4.** Bisect CE at the point F (1.10), so that CF = FE. I say that F is the centre of the circle ABC.

**Step 5.** For suppose it is not. The circle has a centre (D1.16); let G be the centre, G being a point other than F.

**Step 6.** G lies on neither of the straight lines AB, CE. For let XY be either of these two chords and M its point of bisection (M = D for AB, M = F for CE), so that XM = MY, and suppose G lies on XY. Since G is the centre, G lies within the circle (D1.15), hence between X and Y; and GX = GY, both being radii (D1.15). If G were not M, G would lie either between X and M or between M and Y; say between X and M. Then GX is a part of MX and MY is a part of GY, so GX < MX and MY < GY (CN5); but MX = MY; hence GX < GY, contrary to GX = GY. Therefore G = M. Applied to CE this gives G = F, contrary to Step 5; so G is not on CE. Applied to AB it would give G = D, and D lies on CE, which has just been excluded; so G is not on AB either.

**Step 7.** Join GA, GD, GB (P1). Since G is not on AB, ADG and BDG are triangles.

**Step 8.** In the triangles ADG, BDG: AD = DB (Step 2), DG is common, and the base GA equals the base GB, both being straight lines drawn from the centre G to the circumference (D1.15). Therefore the angle ADG, contained by AD, DG, equals the angle BDG, contained by BD, DG (1.8).

**Step 9.** Thus the straight line DG, set up on the straight line AB, makes the adjacent angles ADG, BDG equal to one another; therefore each of them is right (D1.10). In particular the angle GDB is right.

**Step 10.** Since D lies between C and E, the points C, E are on opposite sides of AB; and G, not lying on AB, is on one side of it. Let H be that one of the points C, E which lies on the same side of AB as G. The angle HDB is right: if H = C this is Step 3; if H = E, the angle EDB is vertically opposite to the angle CDA, the straight lines AB and CE cutting one another at D, so that the angle EDB equals the angle CDA (1.15), and the angle CDA is right (Step 3).

**Step 11.** The angles GDB, HDB being both right, the angle GDB equals the angle HDB (P4). But DG and DH are distinct straight lines drawn from D on the same side of AB (G not lying on CE, Step 6), so one of the angles GDB, HDB is a part of the other; hence a part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible (CN5).

**Step 12.** Therefore G is not the centre of the circle ABC. In the same way it is shown that no point other than F is the centre. Since the circle has a centre (D1.16), F is the centre of the given circle ABC; which was to be found.

Note on path: the right angle EDB in Step 10 is obtained from vertical angles (1.15) rather than from 1.13, since 1.15 gives the equality directly without a subtraction step.

result.statement: If on the circumference of a circle two points be taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within the circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and let A and B be two points taken at random on its circumference. Join the straight line AB (P1). I say that AB falls within the circle.

**Step 2.** Suppose it does not. Then some point E of AB, lying between A and B, does not fall within the circle; so E lies either on the circumference or outside the circle.

**Step 3.** Take the centre D of the circle ABC (3.1), and join DA, DB, DE (P1).

**Step 4.** Since D is the centre, the straight lines DA and DB, falling upon the circumference from the centre, are equal to one another (D1.15). Therefore triangle DAB is isosceles, and the angles at its base are equal: angle DAB = angle DBA (1.5).

**Step 5.** Since E lies on AB between A and B, angle DAE is the same angle as angle DAB, and angle DBE is the same angle as angle DBA. Hence angle DAE = angle DBE.

**Step 6.** In triangle DAE, the side AE is produced to B; hence the exterior angle DEB is greater than the interior and opposite angle DAE (1.16).

**Step 7.** Combining Steps 5 and 6, angle DEB is greater than angle DBE.

**Step 8.** In triangle DEB, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19): angle DEB is subtended by DB, and angle DBE is subtended by DE. Therefore DB is greater than DE.

**Step 9.** Case (i): E lies on the circumference. Then DE, falling upon the circumference from the centre, is equal to DB (D1.15). This contradicts Step 8, in which DB is greater than DE.

**Step 10.** Case (ii): E lies outside the circle. Since D is within the circle and E is outside it, the straight line DE crosses the circumference at some point F lying between D and E. Then DF is equal to DB (D1.15); but DF is a part of DE, so DF is less than DE (CN5); hence DB is less than DE. This again contradicts Step 8.

**Step 11.** Both cases are impossible. Therefore no point of AB between A and B lies on or outside the circle, and so the straight line AB falls within the circle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and in it let a straight line CD through the centre bisect a straight line AB, not through the centre, at the point F. I say first that CD also cuts AB at right angles.

**Step 2.** Take the centre of the circle ABC [3.1], and let it be E; join EA and EB [P1]. Since AB does not pass through the centre, E does not lie on AB; hence E is distinct from F, and AFE, BFE are triangles.

**Step 3.** Since F bisects AB, AF is equal to FB; and FE is common. Therefore the two sides AF, FE are equal to the two sides BF, FE respectively.

**Step 4.** The base EA is equal to the base EB, since E is the centre and EA, EB are straight lines falling from the centre upon the circumference [D1.15].

**Step 5.** Therefore, the two triangles AFE, BFE having their two sides equal to two sides respectively and their bases equal, the angle AFE is equal to the angle BFE [1.8].

**Step 6.** But when a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right [D1.10]. Therefore each of the angles AFE, BFE is right, and CD, which passes through the centre and bisects AB not through the centre, also cuts it at right angles.

**Step 7.** Next, let CD cut AB at right angles at F. I say that it also bisects AB, that is, that AF is equal to FB.

**Step 8.** With the same construction (E the centre, EA and EB joined), since EA is equal to EB [D1.15], the triangle EAB is isosceles, and therefore the angle EAF is equal to the angle EBF, these being the angles at the base AB [1.5].

**Step 9.** The angle AFE is right and the angle BFE is right, by hypothesis; and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]. Therefore the angle AFE is equal to the angle BFE.

**Step 10.** Thus EAF, EBF are two triangles having two angles equal to two angles respectively, namely the angle EAF to the angle EBF and the angle AFE to the angle BFE, and one side equal to one side, namely EF, which is common to both and subtends one of the equal angles (the angle EAF in the one triangle and the angle EBF in the other). Therefore they have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides [1.26]; hence AF is equal to FB.

**Step 11.** Therefore CD, which passes through the centre and cuts AB not through the centre at right angles, also bisects it. Consequently, if in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another which are not through the centre, they do not bisect one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and in it let AC and BD be two straight lines, neither of which passes through the centre, cutting one another at the point E. Suppose, if possible, that they bisect one another, so that AE = EC and BE = ED.

**Step 2.** Find the centre of the circle ABCD [3.1] and let it be F. Since AC does not pass through the centre, the point E, which lies on AC, is not the centre; so E and F are distinct points. Join the straight line FE [P1].

**Step 3.** FE is a straight line through the centre F, and it bisects at E the straight line AC, which is not through the centre (AE = EC by Step 1). Therefore FE cuts AC at right angles [3.3]; in particular the angle FEA is a right angle.

**Step 4.** Likewise FE is a straight line through the centre which bisects at E the straight line BD, which is not through the centre (BE = ED by Step 1). Therefore FE cuts BD at right angles [3.3]; in particular the angle FEB is a right angle.

**Step 5.** Since the angles FEA and FEB are both right angles, they are equal to one another [P4].

**Step 6.** Now consider the position of these two angles. The straight line FE passes through E, a point of AC lying between A and C, and FE is a different straight line from AC (because F is not on AC); hence A and C lie on opposite sides of the straight line FE. Also, since BD does not pass through F, BD is a different straight line from FE, and the two have only the point E in common; so B, a point of BD distinct from E (as BE = ED and B is not D), does not lie on the straight line FE. Therefore B lies on the same side of FE as exactly one of the points A, C. Because the supposition AE = EC is symmetric in A and C, we may name the extremities of the first line so that B lies on the same side of FE as A.

**Step 7.** The straight lines AC and BD are two distinct straight lines which cut one another at E, so they have no point in common other than E; in particular B does not lie on AC, and hence the straight lines EA and EB, drawn from E on the same side of FE, are distinct. Consequently one of them falls within the angle contained by FE and the other: either EB falls within the angle FEA, so that the angle FEB is a part of the angle FEA, or EA falls within the angle FEB, so that the angle FEA is a part of the angle FEB.

**Step 8.** In either case one of the angles FEA, FEB is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part [CN5]; so the angles FEA and FEB are unequal. This contradicts Step 5, in which they were shown to be equal.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition of Step 1 is impossible, and AC, BD do not bisect one another. Hence, if in a circle two straight lines cut one another which are not through the centre, they do not bisect one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.
result.proof:
## Proposition 3.5
**Statement:** If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.

**Step 1.** Let the circles ABC and CDG cut one another at the points B and C. Suppose, if possible, that the two circles have the same centre, and let that common centre be E.

**Step 2.** Join EC (P1). Since the circles ABC and CDG cut one another, they are two distinct circles whose circumferences do not coincide; hence there is a point F on the circumference of circle ABC which does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG.

**Step 3.** Join EF (P1). Since E, being the centre of circle CDG, lies within that circle, the straight line drawn from E through F and, if F falls within circle CDG, produced in a straight line beyond F (P2), passes out of circle CDG and so meets its circumference; let it meet the circumference of circle CDG at the point G, on the same side of E as F. Because F does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the points F and G are distinct. Thus E, F, G lie on one straight line with F and G on the same side of E, so that one of the straight lines EF, EG is a part of the other: if F lies within circle CDG, EF is a part of EG, and if F lies outside circle CDG, EG is a part of EF.

**Step 4.** Since E is the centre of circle ABC (D1.16), and the points C and F both lie on the circumference of circle ABC, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EF (D1.15).

**Step 5.** Since E is also the centre of circle CDG (D1.16), and the points C and G both lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EG (D1.15).

**Step 6.** Therefore EF is equal to EG, since each of them is equal to EC (CN1).

**Step 7.** But by Step 3 one of EF, EG is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5); so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 8.** Therefore E is not the centre of both circles ABC and CDG. Hence, if two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, P2, D1.15, D1.16, CN1, CN5

result.statement: If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.

**Step 1.** Let the two circles ABC and CDE touch one another at the point C; that is, they meet one another at C and do not cut one another (D3.3). I say that they will not have the same centre.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let F be the centre of both circles. Then F is a point lying within the circle ABC such that all straight lines falling from F upon the circumference of ABC are equal to one another; and likewise F is a point lying within the circle CDE such that all straight lines falling from F upon the circumference of CDE are equal to one another (D1.15, D1.16).

**Step 3.** Join FC (P1). Since C is on the circumference of ABC and F is the centre of ABC, FC is a straight line falling from the centre upon the circumference of ABC; and since C is also on the circumference of CDE and F is the centre of CDE, FC is likewise a straight line falling from the centre upon the circumference of CDE.

**Step 4.** Since ABC and CDE are two circles and not one and the same circle, their circumferences do not wholly coincide; let E be a point on the circumference of one of them, say CDE, which does not lie on the circumference of the other, ABC.

**Step 5.** Join FE (P1). Because F lies within the circle ABC (Step 2), the straight line FE, produced if necessary (P2), meets the circumference of ABC; let it meet it at B. Since E is not on the circumference of ABC (Step 4), E and B are distinct points, and both lie on the same straight line drawn from F and on the same side of F. Hence either E lies between F and B, so that FE is a part of FB, or B lies between F and E, so that FB is a part of FE.

**Step 6.** Since F is the centre of CDE and both C and E are on its circumference, FE is equal to FC (D1.15). Since F is the centre of ABC and both C and B are on its circumference, FB is equal to FC (D1.15).

**Step 7.** Therefore FE is equal to FB, each being equal to the same straight line FC (CN1).

**Step 8.** But by Step 5 one of FE, FB is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5); so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore F is not the centre of both circles. Hence the two circles ABC and CDE which touch one another do not have the same centre. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If on the diameter of a circle a point be taken which is not the centre of the circle, and from the point straight lines fall upon the circle, that will be greatest on which the centre is, the remainder of the same diameter will be least, and of the rest  the nearer to the straight line through the centre is always greater than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall from the point on the circle, one on each side of the least straight line.
result.proof:
## Proposition 3.7
**Statement:** If on the diameter of a circle a point be taken which is not the centre of the circle, and from the point straight lines fall upon the circle, that will be greatest on which the centre is, the remainder of the same diameter will be least, and of the rest the nearer to the straight line through the centre is always greater than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall from the point on the circle, one on each side of the least straight line.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the circle, AD a diameter, and E the centre; by the definition of a diameter (D1.17), E lies on AD and the ends A, D lie on the circumference. Let F be a point of AD other than E. Name the ends of the diameter so that E lies between A and F; then F lies between E and D, the whole AF is made up of AE and EF, and the whole ED is made up of EF and FD. From F let straight lines FB, FC, FG fall upon the circumference, the points B, C, G lying on the same side of AD in this order from A towards D, so that FB is nearer to the line FA through the centre than FC is, and FC nearer than FG; that is, EC falls within the angle BEF and EG falls within the angle CEF. Join BE, CE, GE (P1).

**Step 2.** FA is greater than FB. In the triangle BEF the two sides BE, EF are together greater than BF (1.20). But BE is equal to AE, both being radii (D1.15); hence AE, EF together are greater than BF, and AE, EF together are the whole AF. Therefore AF is greater than BF. The same argument, applied to the triangle XEF, shows that AF is greater than FX for every point X of the circumference not lying on AD.

**Step 3.** FB is greater than FC, and FC than FG. Since EC falls within the angle BEF, the angle CEF is a part of the angle BEF, so the angle BEF is greater than the angle CEF (CN5). Now in the triangles BEF, CEF the side BE is equal to the side CE (D1.15), EF is common, and the angle BEF contained by the equal sides is greater than the angle CEF; therefore the base BF is greater than the base CF (1.24). In the same way, since EG falls within the angle CEF, the angle CEF is greater than the angle GEF (CN5), and in the triangles CEF, GEF, with CE equal to GE (D1.15) and EF common, the base CF is greater than the base GF (1.24). Hence of the straight lines from F the nearer to the straight line through the centre is always greater than the more remote.

**Step 4.** FD is less than FG. In the triangle GEF the two sides GF, FE are together greater than EG (1.20). But EG is equal to ED (D1.15), and ED is made up of EF and FD; hence GF, FE together are greater than EF, FD together. Taking away the common part FE, the remainder GF is greater than the remainder FD (CN3). The same argument, applied to the triangle XEF, shows that FX is greater than FD for every point X of the circumference not lying on AD. Therefore FD is the least of the straight lines from F to the circle. Moreover, since by Step 2 AF is greater than FX and by this step FX is greater than FD, AF is also greater than FD; so FA, on which the centre lies, is the greatest, and FD, the remainder of the same diameter, is the least.

**Step 5.** Two equal straight lines fall from F, one on each side of FD. On the straight line EF and at the point E on it, construct the angle FEH equal to the angle GEF (1.23), on the other side of AD from G, and let EH meet the circumference at H; join FH (P1). In the triangles GEF, HEF the side GE is equal to the side HE (D1.15), EF is common, and the angle GEF is equal to the angle HEF by construction; therefore the base GF is equal to the base HF (1.4). Thus FG, FH are two equal straight lines from F to the circle, one on each side of the least straight line FD.

**Step 6.** No other straight line from F to the circle is equal to FG. Suppose, if possible, that FK, drawn from F to a point K of the circumference other than G and H, is equal to FG. K is neither A nor D, since FA is greater than FG and FD is less than FG (Steps 2 and 4); so K lies on one side of AD. If K lies on the side of G, consider FG; if on the side of H, then FK is equal to FH, since each is equal to FG (CN1), and the argument below applies with H in place of G. Since K and G are distinct points of the circumference on the same side of AD, each at a distance from E equal to the radius, the straight lines EK and EG are distinct, and one of them falls within the angle that the other makes with EF; so the angles KEF, GEF are unequal, one being a part of the other (CN5). Then in the triangles KEF, GEF the side EK is equal to the side EG (D1.15), EF is common, and the angles at E contained by the equal sides are unequal; therefore the bases FK, FG are unequal, the one opposite the greater angle being the greater (1.24). This contradicts the supposition that FK is equal to FG. Hence only the two straight lines FG, FH, equal to one another, fall from F upon the circle, one on each side of the least straight line FD.

Therefore, of the straight lines from F to the circle, FA on which the centre lies is greatest, FD the remainder of the diameter is least, the nearer to FA is always greater than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines fall from F on the circle, one on each side of FD. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, CN1, CN3, CN5, D1.15, D1.17, 1.4, 1.20, 1.23, 1.24

result.statement: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point straight lines be drawn through to the circle, one of which is through the centre and the others are drawn at random, then, of the straight lines which fall on the concave circumference, that through the centre is greatest, while of the rest   the nearer to that through the centre is always greater than the more remote, but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference, that between the point and the diameter is least, while of the rest the nearer to the least is always less than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall on the circle from the point, one on each side of the least.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle and D a point taken outside it. From D let straight lines DA, DE, DF, DC be drawn through to the circle, DA through the centre and the others at random, so that they meet the concave circumference at A, E, F, C and the convex circumference at G, K, L, H respectively (G on DA, K on DE, L on DF, H on DC), the lines lying on one side of DA with DE nearer to DA than DF, and DF nearer than DC. Let the centre M of the circle ABC be taken [3.1]; M lies on the straight line DA between G and A, so that DA is DM together with MA, and DM is DG together with GM. Join ME, MF, MC, MK, ML, MH [P1].

**Step 2.** (DA is the greatest of the straight lines falling on the concave circumference.) In the triangle EMD the two sides EM, MD are together greater than ED [1.20]. But EM is equal to AM, both being radii of the circle [D1.15]; therefore AM, MD together are greater than ED. But AM, MD together are the whole DA, since M lies on DA. Therefore DA is greater than DE. In the same manner DA is greater than DF and than DC, and than every straight line from D to the concave circumference; therefore DA is the greatest.

**Step 3.** (Of the rest, the nearer to DA is greater than the more remote.) In the triangles EMD, FMD the side EM is equal to the side FM [D1.15], MD is common, and, since DE is nearer to the line through the centre than DF, the angle EMD is greater than the angle FMD. Therefore, two sides being equal to two sides and the included angle greater, the base ED is greater than the base FD [1.24]. In the same manner, in the triangles FMD, CMD, FM is equal to CM, MD is common, and the angle FMD is greater than the angle CMD; therefore FD is greater than CD [1.24].

**Step 4.** (DG is the least of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference.) In the triangle MKD the two sides MK, KD are together greater than MD [1.20]. But MK is equal to MG [D1.15], and MD is MG together with GD; therefore MG, KD together are greater than MG, GD together. Let MG be subtracted from each; therefore the remainder KD is greater than the remainder GD [CN3]. Thus DG is less than DK, and in the same way DG is less than DL and than DH; therefore DG is the least.

**Step 5.** (Of the rest, the nearer to DG is less than the more remote.) Since DK is nearer to DG than DL, the point K falls within the triangle MLD, so that MK, KD are two straight lines constructed from the extremities M, D of the side MD and meeting within the triangle MLD. Therefore MK, KD together are less than the remaining two sides ML, LD together [1.21]. But MK is equal to ML [D1.15]; subtracting these equals, the remainder KD is less than the remainder LD [CN3]. In the same manner L falls within the triangle MHD, so that ML, LD together are less than MH, HD together [1.21]; and ML is equal to MH [D1.15]; therefore LD is less than HD [CN3]. Thus DK is less than DL, and DL less than DH.

**Step 6.** (Two equal straight lines fall from D on the circle, one on each side of DG.) At the point M on the straight line MD, on the other side of DA from K, let the angle DMB be constructed equal to the angle DMK [1.23], the straight line MB being terminated at the point B of the circumference, and let DB be joined [P1]. Then in the triangles KMD, BMD the side MK is equal to the side MB, both being radii [D1.15], MD is common, and the angle KMD is equal to the angle BMD; therefore the base DK is equal to the base DB [1.4]. Thus DK, DB are two equal straight lines falling from D on the circle, one on each side of the least DG.

**Step 7.** (No other straight line equal to DK falls from D on the circle.) If possible, let another straight line DN, equal to DK, fall from D on the convex circumference, N being a point different from K and from B. Since DN is equal to DK, and DK is equal to DB, DN is equal to DB [CN1]. Now N lies on one side of DG. If N lies on the same side as B, then DN, DB are two straight lines falling on the convex circumference on the same side of DG, and one of them is nearer to DG than the other; therefore by Step 5 the nearer is less than the more remote, so that DN is not equal to DB, which is absurd. If N lies on the same side as K, then in the same way DN is not equal to DK, which is absurd. Therefore no straight line other than DK, DB and equal to them falls from D on the circle, and only two equal straight lines fall on the circle from D, one on each side of the least. (The same construction and reasoning, using Step 3 in place of Step 5, gives the corresponding result for a straight line falling on the concave circumference.)

**USED:** 3.1, P1, D1.15, 1.20, 1.24, CN3, 1.21, 1.23, 1.4, CN1

result.statement: If a point be taken within a circle, and more than two equal straight lines fall from the point on the circle, the point taken is the centre of the circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and let D be a point taken within it, from which more than two equal straight lines fall upon the circle; let three of them be DA, DB, DC, so that DA = DB = DC. I say that D is the centre of the circle ABC.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that D is not the centre. Find the centre of the circle ABC [3.1] and let it be E; then E is a point distinct from D.

**Step 3.** Join DE [P1], and produce DE in both directions [P2] until it meets the circumference at the points F and G. Since FG is drawn through the centre E and is terminated in both directions by the circumference, FG is a diameter of the circle ABC [D1.17].

**Step 4.** Thus D is a point on the diameter FG which is not the centre of the circle. Therefore, by 3.7, of the straight lines falling from D upon the circle, only two are equal to one another, one on each side of the least straight line (the shorter of DF, DG).

**Step 5.** But, by hypothesis, the three straight lines DA, DB, DC fall from D upon the circle and are all equal to one another; that is, more than two equal straight lines fall from D on the circle. This contradicts Step 4.

**Step 6.** Therefore the supposition that D is not the centre is impossible; hence the point D is the centre of the circle ABC. Q.E.D.

Path note: a constructive route (bisect AB and BC, show via 1.8 and D1.10 that the lines through D and the midpoints are perpendicular to the chords, then invoke the porism to 3.1 to place the centre on both) is also available; the reductio via 3.7 was chosen as the more direct, since the last clause of 3.7 is precisely the denial of the hypothesis.

result.statement: A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.
result.proof:
## Proposition 3.10
**Statement:** A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.

**Step 1.** For, if possible, let the circle ABC cut the circle DEF at more points than two, and let B, G, H be three of the points at which the circles cut one another. Then each of B, G, H lies on the circumference of the circle ABC and also on the circumference of the circle DEF.

**Step 2.** The points B, G, H are not in one straight line. For if they were, one of them, say G, would lie on the straight line joining the other two, B and H. But B and H are points on the circumference of the circle ABC, so the straight line BH falls within the circle ABC [3.2]; hence G would fall within the circle ABC, whereas it is on the circumference. Therefore B, G, H are not in one straight line.

**Step 3.** Join BG and GH [P1]. By Step 2 these are two distinct straight lines, and since two straight lines cannot enclose a space, they have no point in common except G.

**Step 4.** Bisect BG at the point L and GH at the point M [1.10]. L is a point of BG other than B and G, and M is a point of GH other than G and H. Moreover L and M are distinct points; for otherwise L would be a point common to the straight lines BG and GH other than G, contrary to Step 3.

**Step 5.** From the point L draw LA at right angles to BG, and from the point M draw MC at right angles to GH [1.11], and produce the straight lines AL and CM continuously in both directions [P2].

**Step 6.** The straight lines AL and CM are distinct. For if they were one and the same straight line, then L and M would be two distinct points on it (Step 4), and the straight lines GL and GM drawn from the point G would each make a right angle with it (Step 5); thus in the triangle GLM the two angles GLM, GML would together be equal to two right angles, which is impossible, since in any triangle two angles taken together are less than two right angles [1.17].

**Step 7.** Since AL and CM are distinct straight lines, and two straight lines cannot enclose a space, AL and CM have at most one point in common.

**Step 8.** Let K be the centre of the circle ABC [3.1]. Since in the circle ABC the straight line AL cuts the straight line BG into two equal parts and at right angles (Steps 4 and 5), the centre K of the circle ABC is on AL [3.1, Porism]. Again, since in the circle ABC the straight line CM cuts the straight line GH into two equal parts and at right angles, the centre K is also on CM [3.1, Porism]. Therefore K is a point common to AL and CM.

**Step 9.** Let P be the centre of the circle DEF [3.1]. Since B, G, H are also on the circumference of the circle DEF, BG and GH are straight lines in the circle DEF, and AL cuts BG into two equal parts and at right angles, while CM cuts GH into two equal parts and at right angles; therefore the centre P of the circle DEF is on AL and also on CM [3.1, Porism]. Thus P is likewise a point common to AL and CM.

**Step 10.** But AL and CM have at most one point in common (Step 7). Therefore K and P are one and the same point.

**Step 11.** Hence the circles ABC and DEF, which cut one another, have the same centre; which is impossible, for if two circles cut one another they do not have the same centre [3.5].

**Step 12.** Therefore the circle ABC does not cut the circle DEF at more points than two. Hence a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, P2, 1.10, 1.11, 1.17, 3.1, 3.2, 3.5

result.statement: If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.
result.proof:
## Proposition 3.11
**Statement:** If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.

**Step 1.** Let the circles ABC and ADE touch one another internally at the point A, the circle ADE lying within the circle ABC. By D3.3 the two circles meet one another but do not cut one another; hence A is their only common point, and every point of the circle ADE other than A lies within the circle ABC.

**Step 2.** Let F be the centre of the circle ABC and G the centre of the circle ADE [3.1]. Since the circles touch one another, they do not have the same centre [3.6]; therefore F and G are distinct points.

**Step 3.** Join FG [P1] and produce it in both directions [P2]. Since this straight line passes through the centre F of the circle ABC, it is terminated on each side by the circumference of ABC, and so it is a diameter of the circle ABC [D1.17]. Let H be the extremity of this diameter on the side of G, so that G lies between F and H. Thus G is a point on a diameter of the circle ABC which is not the centre (Step 2).

**Step 4.** I say that the straight line FG, so produced, falls on A. For suppose, if possible, that it does not pass through A. Since G is the centre of the circle ADE, the straight line GH drawn from the centre meets the circumference of ADE at a point D. By the supposition D is not A, and therefore D lies within the circle ABC (Step 1). Hence D falls between G and H on the straight line GH, and GD is a part of GH.

**Step 5.** Therefore GD is less than GH [CN5].

**Step 6.** Join AG [P1]. Since G is a point on the diameter FH of the circle ABC which is not the centre, and GH is the remainder of that diameter, GH is the least of all the straight lines falling from G upon the circle ABC [3.7]. Now AG is a straight line falling from G upon the circle ABC at the point A, and A is not H, because by the supposition the straight line FGH does not pass through A. Therefore AG is greater than GH.

**Step 7.** But G is the centre of the circle ADE, and the points A and D both lie on its circumference; therefore AG is equal to GD [D1.15].

**Step 8.** Consequently GD is greater than GH (Steps 6 and 7). But GD is less than GH (Step 5). Thus the less would be greater than the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition is false, and the straight line joining the centres F and G, when produced, does not fail to pass through A. That is, it falls on A, the point of contact of the circles. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the inequality AG > GH of Step 6 could also be obtained from the triangle AFG by 1.20 (AG + GF > AF = FH = FG + GH, and then removing the common part FG). The route through 3.7 was chosen because 3.7 gives the required inequality directly in a single step for exactly this configuration (a non-central point on a diameter), making the proof the most direct.

**USED:** D3.3, 3.1, 3.6, P1, P2, D1.17, 3.7, D1.15, CN5

result.statement: If two circles touch one another externally, the straight line joining their centres will pass through the point of contact.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the two circles ABC and ADE touch one another externally at the point A. Let F be the centre of the circle ABC and G the centre of the circle ADE [3.1]. I say that the straight line joining F to G passes through A.

**Step 2.** Join FG [P1]. Suppose, if possible, that FG does not pass through A.

**Step 3.** Since the circles touch one another externally, they meet at A but do not cut one another [D3.3]; each circle lies wholly outside the other except at the point of contact A. The point F, being the centre of ABC, lies within circle ABC; the point G, being the centre of ADE, lies within circle ADE and therefore outside circle ABC. Hence the straight line FG, passing from a point inside circle ABC to a point outside it, meets the circumference of ABC at some point C between F and G. Similarly FG meets the circumference of ADE at some point D between F and G. Since FG does not pass through A, neither C nor D is the point A.

**Step 4.** The point D lies on circle ADE and is not A; since the circles do not cut one another [D3.3], D lies outside circle ABC, so FD is greater than the radius FC, and C lies between F and D. Likewise C lies on circle ABC and is not A, so C lies outside circle ADE, GC is greater than the radius GD, and D lies between C and G. Therefore the points lie on FG in the order F, C, D, G, and the segments FC and DG are non-overlapping parts of FG.

**Step 5.** Join FA and AG [P1]. Since A does not lie on FG, the points F, A, G are not in a straight line, and FAG is a triangle.

**Step 6.** Since F is the centre of circle ABC and the points A, C lie on its circumference, FA is equal to FC [D1.15]. Since G is the centre of circle ADE and the points A, D lie on its circumference, GA is equal to GD [D1.15].

**Step 7.** Therefore FA together with AG is equal to FC together with GD [CN2].

**Step 8.** But FC together with GD is a part of the whole FG, since FC and DG are non-overlapping parts of FG and the segment CD remains over. Therefore FG is greater than FC together with GD [CN5], and hence FG is greater than FA together with AG.

**Step 9.** But in the triangle FAG the two sides FA, AG are together greater than the remaining side FG [1.20]; that is, FG is less than FA together with AG.

**Step 10.** Thus FG is both greater than and less than FA together with AG, which is impossible. Therefore the supposition that FG does not pass through A is false, and FG passes through A.

**Step 11.** Therefore, if two circles touch one another externally, the straight line joining their centres will pass through the point of contact. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Suppose, if possible, that the circle ABDC touches the circle EBFD internally at more points than one, say at the points B and D. Let G be the centre of the circle ABDC and H the centre of the circle EBFD (3.1).

**Step 2.** Since the two circles touch one another internally, the straight line joining their centres G and H, when produced, falls on the point of contact (3.11). As both B and D are points of contact, the straight line GH produced passes through both B and D; hence the points B, G, H, D all lie on one straight line.

**Step 3.** This straight line, drawn through the centre G and produced in both directions, is terminated by the circumference of the circle ABDC at B and D, so that BD is a diameter of the circle ABDC and G lies between B and D (D1.17); in the same way BD is a diameter of the circle EBFD and H lies between B and D. Moreover, since the circles touch one another, G and H are not the same point (3.6). Thus G and H are two distinct points of BD, each lying between B and D; let H be the one nearer to D, so that the points lie in the order B, G, H, D. (If G is the nearer, the same reasoning applies with the roles of the two circles interchanged.)

**Step 4.** Since G is the centre of the circle ABDC and the points B, D lie on its circumference, BG is equal to GD (D1.15).

**Step 5.** Since H lies between G and D, HD is a part of GD; therefore GD is greater than HD (CN5). Hence, by Step 4, BG is greater than HD.

**Step 6.** Since G lies between B and H, BG is a part of BH; therefore BH is greater than BG (CN5). Consequently BH is much greater than HD.

**Step 7.** But H is the centre of the circle EBFD and the points B, D lie on its circumference; therefore BH is equal to HD (D1.15). This contradicts Step 6. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle internally at more points than one.

**Step 8.** Next suppose, if possible, that the circle ACK touches the circle ABDC externally at more points than one, say at the points A and C. Join AC (P1).

**Step 9.** Since the points A and C lie on the circumference of the circle ABDC, the straight line AC joining them falls within the circle ABDC (3.2).

**Step 10.** Likewise, since the points A and C lie on the circumference of the circle ACK, the straight line AC falls within the circle ACK (3.2).

**Step 11.** But the circles touch one another externally: they meet without cutting one another (D3.3), and each lies wholly outside the other, so that whatever falls within the circle ABDC falls outside the circle ACK. Hence AC, which by Step 9 falls within the circle ABDC, falls outside the circle ACK. This contradicts Step 10. Therefore a circle does not touch a circle externally at more points than one.

**Step 12.** Therefore a circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In a circle equal straight lines are equally distant from the centre, and those which are equally distant from the centre are equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Statement:** In a circle equal straight lines are equally distant from the centre, and those which are equally distant from the centre are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABDC be a circle, and let AB and CD be straight lines in it (neither through the centre). Let the centre E of the circle be found [3.1]. From E draw EF perpendicular to AB, meeting it at F, and EG perpendicular to CD, meeting it at G [1.12]. Join AE and EC [P1].

**Step 2.** EF is a straight line through the centre cutting the straight line AB, which is not through the centre, at right angles; therefore it also bisects AB [3.3], so AF = FB. Likewise EG bisects CD [3.3], so CG = GD. Hence AB is double of AF and CD is double of CG.

**Step 3.** Since E is the centre and A, C lie on the circumference, AE = EC [D1.15].

**Step 4.** Since the angle AFE is right, in the right-angled triangle AFE the square on AE is equal to the squares on AF and FE together: AE² = AF² + FE² [1.47]. Likewise, since the angle CGE is right, EC² = CG² + GE² [1.47].

**Step 5.** Since AE = EC (Step 3), AE² = EC²; therefore AF² + FE² = CG² + GE² [CN1]. This relation holds for any two chords AB, CD of the circle, and both parts of the proposition follow from it.

**Step 6.** (First part.) Suppose AB = CD. Then their halves are equal (Step 2): AF = CG, and so AF² = CG².

**Step 7.** Subtracting the equals AF², CG² from the equals AF² + FE², CG² + GE² of Step 5, the remainders are equal: FE² = GE² [CN3]. Therefore FE = GE.

**Step 8.** FE and GE are the perpendiculars drawn from the centre E to AB and CD respectively, and they are equal; therefore AB and CD are equally distant from the centre [D3.4]. This proves the first part.

**Step 9.** (Second part.) Now suppose instead that AB and CD are equally distant from the centre, that is, the perpendiculars FE and GE from the centre to them are equal [D3.4]: FE = GE, and so FE² = GE².

**Step 10.** Subtracting the equals FE², GE² from the equals AF² + FE², CG² + GE² of Step 5, the remainders are equal: AF² = CG² [CN3]. Therefore AF = CG.

**Step 11.** By Step 2, FB = AF and GD = CG; since AF = CG, also FB = GD [CN1]. Adding equals to equals, AF + FB = CG + GD, that is, AB = CD [CN2]. This proves the second part.

**Step 12.** Therefore in a circle equal straight lines are equally distant from the centre, and those which are equally distant from the centre are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the first part could alternatively be obtained by congruence (triangles AEB, CED by 1.8, then triangles AFE, CGE by 1.26), but the converse would still require 1.47, so the single route through 1.47 and 3.3 is the more direct and uniform choice.

result.statement: Of straight lines in a circle the diameter is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the centre is always greater than the more remote.
result.proof:
**Statement:** Of straight lines in a circle the diameter is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the centre is always greater than the more remote.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle with centre E, and let AD be a diameter of it; by D1.17 the diameter AD passes through the centre E, so that E lies on AD and AD is made up of AE and ED. Let BC and FG be any two straight lines in the circle not through the centre, and let BC be nearer to the centre than FG. It is to be proved that AD is greater than BC, and that BC is greater than FG.

**Step 2.** From the centre E draw EH perpendicular to BC and EK perpendicular to FG (1.12). Since BC is nearer to the centre and FG more remote, the perpendicular falling on FG is the greater (D3.5); therefore EK is greater than EH.

**Step 3.** From the greater EK cut off EL equal to the less EH (1.3); since EL = EH < EK, the point L falls between E and K. Through L draw LM at right angles to EK (1.11), and produce it in both directions (P2) so that it meets the circumference at M and N. Join EM, EN, EF, EG, EB, EC (P1).

**Step 4.** The perpendicular from the centre E on MN is EL (for MN is at right angles to EK at L), and the perpendicular from E on BC is EH; and EL = EH by construction. Therefore BC and MN are equally distant from the centre (D3.4), and hence BC is equal to MN (3.14).

**Step 5.** Since E is the centre, AE = EB and ED = EC (D1.15). Adding these equals, AE + ED = EB + EC (CN2); that is, AD = EB + EC. But in the triangle EBC the two sides EB, EC together are greater than the third side BC (1.20). Therefore AD, being equal to EB + EC, is greater than BC. Since BC was any straight line in the circle not through the centre, the diameter AD is greatest.

**Step 6.** Consider the triangles MEN and FEG. Since E is the centre, ME = FE and EN = EG (D1.15). Moreover, because L lies between E and K, the points F, G lie on the far side of MN from E, so the straight lines EF and EG cross MN at points between M and N; hence EF and EG fall within the angle MEN, and the angle FEG is a part of the angle MEN. Therefore the angle MEN is greater than the angle FEG (CN5).

**Step 7.** Thus in the triangles MEN and FEG the two sides ME, EN are equal to the two sides FE, EG respectively, and the angle MEN contained by the equal sides is greater than the angle FEG. Therefore the base MN is greater than the base FG (1.24).

**Step 8.** But MN was proved equal to BC (Step 4). Therefore BC is greater than FG. Hence of straight lines in a circle the diameter AD is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the centre, BC, is greater than the more remote, FG. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D1.17, D1.15, D3.4, D3.5, 1.12, 1.3, 1.11, P1, P2, 3.14, CN2, 1.20, CN5, 1.24

result.statement: The straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle.
result.proof:
## Proposition 3.16
**Statement:** The straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle with centre D, let AB be a diameter of it, so that AB passes through D (D1.17), and let AE be the straight line drawn from the extremity A at right angles to AB, so that the angle BAE, which is the same as the angle DAE, is a right angle (D1.10). Let CHA be the circumference of the semicircle on the side of E, the semicircle being contained by the diameter BA and the circumference CHA (D1.18).

**Step 2.** I say first that AE falls outside the circle. For, if not, some point of AE other than A lies within the circle or upon the circumference; in either case AE (produced if necessary, P2) falls within the circle and meets the circumference again at a point C other than A. Join DC (P1).

**Step 3.** Since D is the centre, DA is equal to DC (D1.15). Therefore, in the isosceles triangle DAC, the angle DAC is equal to the angle DCA (1.5).

**Step 4.** But the angle DAC is the angle which AE makes with AB at A, and is therefore right. Hence the angle DCA is also right, and the two angles DAC, DCA of the triangle DAC are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 5.** This is impossible, for in any triangle two angles taken together are less than two right angles (1.17). Therefore no point of AE other than A lies within the circle or on the circumference: the straight line drawn from A at right angles to AB falls outside the circle.

**Step 6.** I say next that into the space between the straight line AE and the circumference CHA another straight line cannot be interposed. For, if possible, let a straight line FA drawn from A be so interposed; that is, FA lies within the angle BAE, and every point of FA except A is outside the circle. Since FA lies between AE and the circumference, the angle DAF is a part of the right angle DAE, and so the angle DAF is less than a right angle (CN5).

**Step 7.** The point D is not on FA, since D is within the circle while FA lies outside it except for A. From D draw DG perpendicular to FA (1.12), meeting it at G; then the angle AGD is right (D1.10). G is not the point A, for then DA would be perpendicular to FA and the angle DAF would be right, contrary to Step 6. Hence DAG is a triangle, and, the angle AGD being right, the angle DAG is less than a right angle (1.17).

**Step 8.** Moreover, G lies on FA on the side of F. For if G lay on FA produced beyond A, the angles DAG, DAF would be the adjacent angles made by DA standing on the straight line GAF, and so would together equal two right angles (1.13); but each of them is less than a right angle (Steps 6, 7). Therefore G is a point of FA other than A, and consequently G lies outside the circle.

**Step 9.** In the triangle AGD the angle AGD, being right, is greater than the angle DAG, which is less than a right angle; and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19). Therefore AD is greater than DG.

**Step 10.** Since D is within the circle and G is outside it, the straight line DG meets the circumference at a point H lying between D and G. Thus DH is a part of DG, and DG is greater than DH (CN5).

**Step 11.** But DH is equal to DA, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference (D1.15), and DA is greater than DG (Step 9); therefore DH is greater than DG, the less than the greater, which contradicts Step 10. Therefore another straight line cannot be interposed into the space between the straight line AE and the circumference CHA.

**Step 12.** Before proving the last part, observe the following. Let AF be any straight line drawn from A within the angle BAE. If every point of AF other than A were outside the circle, AF would be interposed between AE and the circumference CHA, which is impossible (Step 11). Hence some point of AF other than A lies within the circle or on the circumference, and AF (produced if necessary, P2) meets the circumference again at a point C other than A; and the straight line AC, joining two points of the circumference, falls within the circle (3.2). Thus every straight line AF drawn from A within the angle BAE falls within the circle; consequently the circumference CHA lies between AF and AE, so that the angle BAF is a part of the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA, and the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE is a part of the rectilineal angle FAE.

**Step 13.** Now let K be any acute rectilineal angle, so that K is less than a right angle (D1.12) and therefore less than the right angle BAE (P4). On the straight line AB, at the point A on it, construct the angle BAF equal to K (1.23), on the same side of AB as E. Since the angle BAF is less than the angle BAE, AF falls within the angle BAE; hence by Step 12 the angle BAF is a part of the angle contained by BA and the circumference CHA. Therefore the angle of the semicircle, namely the angle contained by the straight line BA and the circumference CHA (D3.7), is greater than the angle BAF (CN5), that is, greater than K.

**Step 14.** Again, on the straight line AE, at the point A on it, construct the angle EAF equal to K (1.23), on the same side of AE as B. Since the angle EAF is less than the right angle EAB (P4), AF falls within the angle BAE; hence by Step 12 the angle contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE is a part of the angle EAF. Therefore the remaining angle, contained by the circumference CHA and the straight line AE (D3.7), is less than the angle EAF (CN5), that is, less than K.

**Step 15.** Since K was any acute rectilineal angle, the angle of the semicircle is greater than any acute rectilineal angle, and the remaining angle is less than any acute rectilineal angle. Therefore the straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity falls outside the circle; into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; and the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle. Q.E.D.

*Remark on path.* For the third part the argument is direct: an angle equal to the given acute angle is constructed at A (1.23), the constructed line is shown to fall within the circle by the second part together with 3.2, and the comparison follows from the part–whole relation (CN5). This is the most immediate route, since it uses the second part exactly as already proved rather than a reductio from the converse of the part–whole relation.

**USED:** P1, P2, P4, CN5, D1.10, D1.12, D1.15, D1.17, D1.18, D3.7, 1.5, 1.12, 1.13, 1.17, 1.19, 1.23, 3.2

result.statement: From a given point to draw a straight line touching a given circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given point (taken outside the circle) and BCD the given circle. Take the centre E of the circle BCD [3.1], and join AE [P1]. Since A lies outside the circle and E within it, the straight line AE crosses the circumference; let it meet the circumference of the circle BCD at D.

**Step 2.** With centre E and distance EA describe the circle AFG [P3].

**Step 3.** From the point D draw DF at right angles to EA [1.11]; since D lies within the circle AFG (ED being less than EA), let DF, produced as required, meet the circumference of the circle AFG at F.

**Step 4.** Join EF and let it meet the circumference of the circle BCD at B; join AB [P1].

**Step 5.** Since E is the centre of the circle AFG, EA is equal to EF [D1.15]; and since E is the centre of the circle BCD, ED is equal to EB [D1.15].

**Step 6.** Therefore in the triangles AEB, FED the two sides AE, EB are equal to the two sides FE, ED respectively, and they contain the common angle at E. Therefore the base AB is equal to the base FD, the triangle AEB is equal to the triangle FED, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles, namely those which the equal sides subtend; in particular the angle EBA is equal to the angle EDF [1.4].

**Step 7.** But the angle EDF is right, since DF was drawn at right angles to EA (Step 3). Therefore the angle EBA is also right.

**Step 8.** Now EB is drawn from the centre E to the circumference at B; produce BE through E to meet the circumference again [P2], so that the straight line so obtained, passing through the centre and terminated in both directions by the circumference, is a diameter of the circle BCD [D1.17], of which B is an extremity.

**Step 9.** Thus AB is a straight line drawn at right angles to a diameter of the circle BCD from its extremity B. Therefore AB falls outside the circle BCD [3.16]; that is, AB meets the circle at B and, being produced, does not cut it.

**Step 10.** Therefore AB touches the circle BCD [D3.2]. Hence from the given point A the straight line AB has been drawn touching the given circle BCD, which was to be done.

result.statement: If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, let the centre F of the circle ABC be taken (3.1), and let FC be joined from F to C (P1). I say that FC is perpendicular to DE.

**Step 2.** Suppose that FC is not perpendicular to DE. The centre F lies within the circle, and DE, since it touches the circle, does not cut it (D3.2); hence F is not on DE. From F draw FG perpendicular to DE, DE being regarded as produced as far as necessary (1.12), and let G be the foot of this perpendicular on DE. The point G is not the point C: for if G coincided with C, the perpendicular FG would be the very line FC, and FC would be perpendicular to DE, contrary to the supposition.

**Step 3.** Since FG is perpendicular to DE, the angle FGC is right (D1.10). In the triangle FGC the two angles FGC and FCG together are less than two right angles (1.17); since the angle FGC is itself a right angle, the angle FCG is less than a right angle. Therefore the angle FGC is greater than the angle FCG.

**Step 4.** In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19). In the triangle FGC the side FC subtends the greater angle FGC and the side FG subtends the lesser angle FCG; therefore FC is greater than FG.

**Step 5.** Since DE touches the circle ABC, it meets the circle and, being produced, does not cut the circle (D3.2). Moreover DE meets the circle at no point other than C: for if it met the circle at a second point H, the straight line CH joining two points of the circumference would fall within the circle (3.2), so that DE would cut the circle, contrary to D3.2. Hence G, being a point of DE different from C, lies neither on the circumference nor within the circle; that is, G lies outside the circle.

**Step 6.** The centre F lies within the circle and G lies outside it; therefore the straight line FG passes across the circumference. Let FG meet the circumference at the point B. Then FB is a part of FG, so that FG is greater than FB (CN5).

**Step 7.** Since F is the centre and B, C are points on the circumference, FB is equal to FC (D1.15). By Step 4, FC is greater than FG; hence FB, being equal to FC, is also greater than FG. But by Step 6, FG is greater than FB. Thus FB would be at once greater than and less than FG, which is impossible.

**Step 8.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false, and FC is perpendicular to DE. Hence, if a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined is perpendicular to the tangent. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line DE touch the circle ABC at the point C, and from C let CA be drawn at right angles to DE, so that the adjacent angles ACD and ACE are each right (D1.10). We must show that the centre of the circle ABC lies on CA.

**Step 2.** Suppose it does not. Let F be the centre of the circle ABC, F not lying on CA, and join CF (P1).

**Step 3.** Since DE touches the circle ABC at C, and FC has been joined from the centre F to the point of contact C, FC is perpendicular to DE (3.18); therefore each of the angles FCD and FCE is right (D1.10).

**Step 4.** But the angle ACE is also right (Step 1). Therefore the angle FCE is equal to the angle ACE, since all right angles are equal to one another (P4). Likewise the angle FCD is equal to the angle ACD (P4).

**Step 5.** Now, since F does not lie on CA, the straight line CF is distinct from CA, and so CF falls within one of the two angles ACE and ACD which CA makes with DE at C. If CF falls within the angle ACE, then the angle FCE is a part of the angle ACE, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5), so the angle ACE is greater than the angle FCE; but by Step 4 they are equal, which is impossible. If instead CF falls within the angle ACD, then in the same way the angle ACD is greater than the angle FCD (CN5), while by Step 4 they are equal, which is impossible.

**Step 6.** Therefore F is not the centre of the circle ABC. Similarly we can prove that no point other than a point on CA is the centre. Therefore the centre of the circle ABC is on the straight line CA drawn from the point of contact at right angles to the tangent DE.

Therefore, if a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In a circle the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference, when the angles have the same circumference as base.
result.proof:
**Statement:** In a circle the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference, when the angles have the same circumference as base.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle with centre E. Let the angle BEC be an angle at the centre and the angle BAC an angle at the circumference, and let both stand on the same circumference BC as base. I say that the angle BEC is double of the angle BAC.

**Step 2.** Join AE [P1] and produce it in a straight line beyond E to a point F [P2].

**Step 3.** Since E is the centre of the circle, the straight lines EA, EB, EC drawn from E to the circumference are equal to one another; thus EA = EB and EA = EC [D1.15].

**Step 4.** Case 1: the straight line AF falls within the angle BAC. In the triangle ABE, since EA = EB, the angle EAB is equal to the angle EBA [1.5]. Hence the two angles EAB and EBA taken together are double of the angle EAB.

**Step 5.** Since the side AE of the triangle ABE has been produced to F, the exterior angle BEF is equal to the two interior and opposite angles EAB and EBA taken together [1.32]. The angle BEF and the double of the angle EAB are therefore each equal to the same sum, so the angle BEF is double of the angle EAB [CN1].

**Step 6.** In the same way, in the triangle ACE, since EA = EC, the angle EAC is equal to the angle ECA [1.5]; the exterior angle FEC is equal to the two interior and opposite angles EAC and ECA together [1.32]; hence the angle FEC is double of the angle EAC [CN1].

**Step 7.** Adding these equals: the whole angle BEC, which is the sum of the angles BEF and FEC, is double of the whole angle BAC, which is the sum of the angles EAB and EAC [CN2]. Thus in Case 1 the angle BEC is double of the angle BAC.

**Step 8.** Case 2: the straight line through the vertex and the centre falls outside the angle at the circumference. Let the angle BDC at the circumference stand on the same circumference BC, with D so placed that, when DE is joined [P1] and produced to G [P2], the line DG falls outside the angle BDC, the line DB lying between DC and DG. Then the angle BDC is the excess of the angle EDC over the angle EDB, and the angle BEC is the excess of the angle GEC over the angle GEB.

**Step 9.** As before, ED = EC and ED = EB [D1.15]. In the triangle DEC the angle EDC is equal to the angle ECD [1.5], and the exterior angle GEC is equal to the angles EDC and ECD together [1.32]; hence the angle GEC is double of the angle EDC [CN1]. Likewise in the triangle DEB the angle EDB is equal to the angle EBD [1.5], the exterior angle GEB is equal to the angles EDB and EBD together [1.32], and so the angle GEB is double of the angle EDB [CN1].

**Step 10.** Subtracting equals from equals: the remaining angle BEC, which is the angle GEC less the angle GEB, is double of the remaining angle BDC, which is the angle EDC less the angle EDB [CN3]. Thus in Case 2 also the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference.

**Step 11.** Case 3: the straight line through the vertex and the centre coincides with one side of the angle at the circumference, say AB passes through E. Then AE produced beyond E falls along EB, so the angle BEC is itself the exterior angle of the triangle ACE at E, and by Step 6 the angle BEC is double of the angle EAC, that is, of the angle BAC.

**Step 12.** Therefore in every case, in a circle the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference when the angles have the same circumference as base. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and let BAED be a segment of it with base BD. Let A and E be two points taken on the circumference of this segment, and let AB, AD, EB, ED be joined. Then the angles BAD and BED are angles in the same segment BAED, since each is contained by straight lines joined from a point on the circumference of the segment to the extremities B, D of its base (D3.8). I say that the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED.

**Step 2.** Let the centre of the circle ABCD be found, and let it be F (3.1).

**Step 3.** Let BF and FD be joined (P1).

**Step 4.** The straight lines AB, AD containing the angle BAD cut off the circumference BCD, the part of the circle's circumference lying outside the segment BAED; hence the angle BAD stands upon the circumference BCD (D3.9). Likewise the straight lines FB, FD containing the angle BFD cut off the same circumference BCD, so that the angle BFD also stands upon the circumference BCD (D3.9).

**Step 5.** Now the angle BFD is at the centre of the circle and the angle BAD is at the circumference, and they have the same circumference BCD as base; therefore the angle BFD is double of the angle BAD (3.20).

**Step 6.** Again, the straight lines EB, ED containing the angle BED cut off the same circumference BCD (D3.9), so the angle BED at the circumference and the angle BFD at the centre have the same circumference BCD as base; therefore, for the same reason, the angle BFD is also double of the angle BED (3.20).

**Step 7.** Hence the angle BAD is the half of the angle BFD, and the angle BED is also the half of the same angle BFD. Since each of the angles BAD, BED is equal to the half of the same angle BFD, they are equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 8.** Therefore the angle BAD is equal to the angle BED. And since A and E were any two points whatever on the circumference of the segment, the angles in the same segment are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: The opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and let ABCD be a quadrilateral in it, so that its four angular points A, B, C, D lie on the circumference. I say that the opposite angles ABC, ADC are together equal to two right angles, and likewise that the opposite angles BAD, BCD are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** Join the straight lines AC and BD [P1].

**Step 3.** Since in any triangle the three angles are together equal to two right angles [1.32], in the triangle ABC the three angles CAB, ABC, BCA are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 4.** The straight line BC together with the circumference BADC contains a segment of the circle, and A and D are points on that circumference; from A the straight lines AB, AC are joined to the extremities B, C of the base BC, and from D the straight lines DB, DC are joined to the same extremities B, C. Hence the angle BAC and the angle BDC are both angles in the segment BADC [D3.8]. Therefore the angle CAB is equal to the angle BDC, since angles in the same segment of a circle are equal to one another [3.21].

**Step 5.** Likewise the straight line AB together with the circumference ADCB contains a segment of the circle, and C and D are points on that circumference; from C the straight lines CA, CB are joined to the extremities A, B of the base AB, and from D the straight lines DA, DB are joined to the same extremities. Hence the angle ACB and the angle ADB are both angles in the segment ADCB [D3.8]. Therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle ADB [3.21].

**Step 6.** The diagonal DB lies within the angle ADC, so that the whole angle ADC is made up of the two angles ADB, BDC. Adding the equals obtained in Steps 4 and 5, the angles BAC, ACB together are equal to the angles BDC, ADB together, that is, to the whole angle ADC [CN2].

**Step 7.** Let the angle ABC be added to each of these equals; then the three angles ABC, BAC, ACB together are equal to the two angles ABC, ADC together [CN2].

**Step 8.** But the three angles ABC, BAC, ACB are together equal to two right angles (Step 3). Therefore the angles ABC, ADC are together equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 9.** Similarly for the other pair of opposite angles. In the triangle ABD the three angles ABD, BDA, DAB are together equal to two right angles [1.32]. The angle ABD and the angle ACD are angles in the same segment ABCD on the base AD, since B and C lie on the circumference ABCD and the straight lines BA, BD and CA, CD are joined to the extremities A, D [D3.8]; hence the angle ABD is equal to the angle ACD [3.21]. Also, by Step 5, the angle ADB is equal to the angle ACB. The diagonal CA lies within the angle BCD, so the whole angle BCD is made up of the angles ACD, ACB; hence the angles ABD, ADB together are equal to the whole angle BCD [CN2]. Adding the angle DAB to each, the three angles DAB, ABD, ADB together are equal to the two angles DAB, BCD together [CN2]; and the former are equal to two right angles, so the angles BAD, DCB are together equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 10.** Therefore in the quadrilateral ABCD in the circle, each pair of opposite angles is together equal to two right angles. Hence the opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles. Q.E.D.

result.statement: On the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, and suppose, if possible, that on AB two similar and unequal segments of circles, ACB and ADB, have been constructed on the same side of AB. Each segment is the figure contained by the base AB and its circumference (D3.6).

**Step 2.** Since the segments ACB and ADB are unequal, they do not coincide; for things which coincide with one another are equal (CN4). Hence the circumferences ACB and ADB are not the same circumference, and the circles of which they are parts are distinct circles. Both circles pass through the points A and B, so they cut one another at A and at B; and since a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two (3.10), the two circumferences have no common point other than A and B. Both circumferences lie on the same side of AB and have the same extremities A and B; therefore one of them falls entirely within the segment bounded by the other. Let the circumference ACB fall within the segment ADB.

**Step 3.** Take any point C on the circumference ACB other than A and B, join AC (P1), and produce AC beyond C in a straight line (P2). The point C lies within the segment ADB (Step 2). The straight line AC is distinct from AB, since C does not lie on AB; hence AC produced cannot meet AB at any point other than A. Therefore, since the boundary of segment ADB consists only of the base AB and the circumference ADB (D3.6), the produced straight line, leaving the segment ADB, must meet the circumference ADB; let it meet it at D. Thus A, C, D lie in one straight line, with C between A and D.

**Step 4.** Join CB and DB (P1).

**Step 5.** The angle ACB is the angle in the segment ACB, since C is a point on its circumference and CA, CB are joined from C to the extremities A, B of the base (D3.8). Likewise the angle ADB is the angle in the segment ADB (D3.8). Since the segment ACB is similar to the segment ADB, and similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles (D3.11), the angle ACB is equal to the angle ADB.

**Step 6.** Now consider the triangle BCD. Its side DC, when produced beyond C, passes through A (Step 3), so the angle ACB is the exterior angle at C of triangle BCD, contained by BC and the production CA of the side DC. By 1.16, the exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles; therefore the angle ACB is greater than the interior and opposite angle CDB. But the angle CDB is the same angle as ADB, because C lies on the straight line DA. Hence the angle ACB is greater than the angle ADB.

**Step 7.** By Step 5 the angle ACB is equal to the angle ADB, and by Step 6 the angle ACB is greater than the angle ADB. The same angle cannot be both equal to and greater than the angle ADB; this is impossible.

**Step 8.** The supposition of Step 1 therefore leads to an impossibility. Hence on the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, P2, CN4, D3.6, D3.8, D3.11, 1.16, 3.10

result.statement: Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AEB and CFD be similar segments of circles on the equal straight lines AB and CD, where E and F are points on the respective circumferences. By D3.11, since the segments are similar, the angle in the segment AEB is equal to the angle in the segment CFD. It is required to prove that the segment AEB is equal to the segment CFD.

**Step 2.** Apply the segment AEB to the segment CFD so that the point A is placed on the point C and the straight line AB is laid along the straight line CD, with the circumference AEB on the same side of CD as the circumference CFD. Then the point B coincides with the point D. For if B did not coincide with D, then B would fall either between C and D or beyond D; in the first case AB would be a part of CD and so less than CD, and in the second case CD would be a part of AB and so less than AB (CN5); either alternative contradicts the hypothesis that AB is equal to CD. Hence B falls on D, and the straight line AB coincides with the straight line CD.

**Step 3.** I say that the circumference AEB also coincides with the circumference CFD. Suppose it does not. The circumference AEB now has the extremities C and D and lies on the same side of CD as the circumference CFD, so it must either (a) fall entirely within the circumference CFD, or (b) fall entirely outside it, or (c) fall awry, partly within and partly without, crossing the circumference CFD at some point G lying between C and D, as CGD.

**Step 4.** Cases (a) and (b). The transported segment is a segment of a circle on the straight line CD (D3.6), on the same side of CD as the segment CFD, and by Step 1 it admits an angle equal to the angle in CFD, so the two segments are similar (D3.11). If the transported segment falls within CFD, it is a part of CFD, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5), so the two segments are unequal; if it falls outside CFD, then CFD is a part of it, and again by CN5 they are unequal. Thus in either case there would be constructed on the same straight line CD, on the same side, two similar and unequal segments of circles. But this is impossible by 3.23.

**Step 5.** Case (c). The circumference CGD and the circumference CFD, not coinciding, are arcs of two distinct circles, and these two circles meet and cut one another at the three points C, G and D. But a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two (3.10). This also is impossible.

**Step 6.** Since all three cases are impossible, the circumference AEB coincides with the circumference CFD. The segment AEB is the figure contained by the straight line AB and the circumference AEB, and the segment CFD is the figure contained by the straight line CD and the circumference CFD (D3.6). Since AB coincides with CD (Step 2) and the circumference AEB coincides with the circumference CFD, the whole segment AEB coincides with the whole segment CFD.

**Step 7.** Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another (CN4). Therefore the segment AEB is equal to the segment CFD. Hence similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: Given a segment of a circle, to describe the complete circle of which it is a segment.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given segment of a circle, AC its base and ABC its circumference. Bisect AC at the point D (1.10); from D draw DB at right angles to AC (1.11), and let it meet the circumference of the segment at B; join AB (P1).

**Step 2.** In the triangle ABD the angle ADB is right (Step 1), and any two angles of a triangle are together less than two right angles (1.17); hence each of the angles ABD, BAD is less than a right angle. Now the angle ABD is either greater than, equal to, or less than the angle BAD, and we treat the three cases in turn.

**Step 3.** (Case I: angle ABD greater than angle BAD.) On the straight line BA, at the point A on it, construct the angle BAE equal to the angle ABD (1.23), on the same side of AB as D. The angles BAE, ABD are together equal to twice the angle ABD, which is less than two right angles (Step 2); therefore the straight lines AE and BD, produced if necessary (P2), meet on the side of D (P5). Let them meet at E, and join EC (P1). Since the angle BAE is greater than the angle BAD, the line AE falls outside the angle BAD, on the other side of AC from B; so E lies on DB produced beyond D, outside the segment.

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABE the angle ABE is equal to the angle BAE (Step 3); therefore the side AE, which subtends the angle ABE, is equal to the side BE, which subtends the angle BAE (1.6).

**Step 5.** Because B, D, E lie in one straight line, the straight line DA set up on BE makes the angles ADE, ADB together equal to two right angles (1.13); the angle ADB is right (Step 1), so the angle ADE is right. In the same way DC set up on BE makes the angles CDE, CDB together equal to two right angles (1.13), and CDB is right, so CDE is right. Hence the angle ADE is equal to the angle CDE (P4).

**Step 6.** In the triangles ADE, CDE, the side AD is equal to the side DC (Step 1), the side DE is common, and the angle ADE is equal to the angle CDE (Step 5); therefore the base AE is equal to the base CE (1.4).

**Step 7.** AE is equal to BE (Step 4) and AE is equal to CE (Step 6); therefore the three straight lines EA, EB, EC are equal to one another (CN1). With centre E and distance EA describe a circle (P3); since EB and EC are each equal to EA, this circle passes also through B and C (D1.15). Its centre E lies outside the segment, so in this case the segment ABC is less than a semicircle.

**Step 8.** (Case II: angle ABD equal to angle BAD.) Then in the triangle ABD the side DA, subtending the angle ABD, is equal to the side DB, subtending the angle BAD (1.6). But DA is equal to DC (Step 1); therefore DA, DB, DC are equal to one another (CN1). With centre D and distance DA describe a circle (P3); since DB and DC are each equal to DA, it passes through B and C (D1.15). Since AC passes through the centre D, it is a diameter (D1.17), and the segment ABC is a semicircle (D1.18).
