**Step 9.** (Case III: angle ABD less than angle BAD.) On the straight line BA, at the point A on it, construct the angle BAE equal to the angle ABD (1.23), on the same side of AB as D. Exactly as in Step 3, the angles BAE, ABD are together less than two right angles, so AE meets BD at a point E on the side of D (P5); and since the angle BAE is now less than the angle BAD, AE falls within the angle BAD and meets BD between B and D, so E lies within the segment. Join EC (P1).

**Step 10.** As in Step 4, since the angle ABE is equal to the angle BAE, AE is equal to BE (1.6). Here the angles ADE, CDE are the right angles ADB, BDC themselves (Step 1), and so are equal (P4); hence, as in Step 6, since AD is equal to DC, DE is common, and the angle ADE is equal to the angle CDE, the base AE is equal to the base CE (1.4). Therefore EA, EB, EC are equal to one another (CN1); with centre E and distance EA describe a circle (P3), which passes through B and C as well as A (D1.15). Its centre E lies within the segment, so in this case the segment ABC is greater than a semicircle.

**Step 11.** In every case a circle has been described which passes through the three points A, B, C, all of which lie on the circumference of the given segment. Two distinct circles cannot have three points in common, for a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two (3.10); therefore the circle described is the very circle of which ABC is a segment. Given the segment ABC, the complete circle of which it is a segment has therefore been described. Q.E.F.

result.statement: In equal circles equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC, DEF be equal circles with centres G, H. Let the angles BGC, EHF stand at the centres and the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences, the straight lines containing each angle cutting off the circumferences BKC, ELF respectively, so that each of the angles BGC and BAC stands upon the circumference BKC, and each of the angles EHF and EDF stands upon the circumference ELF [D3.9]. Suppose that the angles BGC, EHF at the centres are equal, or that the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences are equal. I say that the circumference BKC is equal to the circumference ELF.

**Step 2.** In the circle ABC the angle BGC at the centre and the angle BAC at the circumference have the same circumference BKC as base; therefore the angle BGC is double of the angle BAC [3.20]. Likewise in the circle DEF the angle EHF at the centre is double of the angle EDF at the circumference, since both have the circumference ELF as base [3.20].

**Step 3.** Hence, if the angles BGC, EHF at the centres are equal, their halves, the angles BAC, EDF, are equal, since the halves of equals are equal; and if the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences are equal, then their doubles, the angles BGC, EHF, are equal, since equals added to equals give equal wholes [CN2]. In either case, therefore, both the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 4.** Join BC, EF [P1].

**Step 5.** Since the circles ABC, DEF are equal, their radii are equal [D3.1]; therefore GB is equal to HE, and GC is equal to HF.

**Step 6.** In the triangles GBC, HEF the two sides GB, GC are equal to the two sides HE, HF respectively, and the angle BGC contained by them is equal to the angle EHF contained by HE, HF (Step 3); therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF [1.4].

**Step 7.** The straight line BC and the circumference BAC contain the segment BAC of the circle ABC, and the straight line EF and the circumference EDF contain the segment EDF of the circle DEF [D3.6]. The angle BAC, contained by the straight lines joined from the point A on the circumference of the segment to the extremities B, C of its base BC, is an angle in the segment BAC; likewise the angle EDF is an angle in the segment EDF [D3.8]. Since these angles are equal (Step 3), the segments BAC, EDF admit equal angles, and are therefore similar segments [D3.11].

**Step 8.** The similar segments BAC, EDF stand on the equal straight lines BC, EF (Step 6); but similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another; therefore the segment BAC is equal to the segment EDF [3.24].

**Step 9.** The whole circle ABC is equal to the whole circle DEF, and the segment BAC is equal to the segment EDF (Step 8); if these equal segments be subtracted from the equal circles, the remainders are equal; therefore the remaining segment BKC is equal to the remaining segment ELF [CN3].

**Step 10.** The equal segments BKC, ELF are contained by the equal bases BC, EF together with the circumferences BKC, ELF respectively; therefore the circumference BKC is equal to the circumference ELF. Thus in the equal circles ABC, DEF the equal angles, whether the angles BGC, EHF at the centres or the angles BAC, EDF at the circumferences, stand on the equal circumferences BKC, ELF, which was to be proved.

result.statement: In equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be equal circles with centres G and H, and let the angles BGC and EHF at the centres, and the angles BAC and EDF at the circumferences, stand on equal circumferences BC and EF. I say that the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF, and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Suppose that the angle BGC is not equal to the angle EHF. Then one of them is greater; let the angle BGC be the greater.

**Step 3.** On the straight line BG and at the point G on it, construct the angle BGK equal to the angle EHF [1.23], and let the side GK meet the circumference of the circle ABC at K. Since the angle BGK is equal to the angle EHF, which is less than the angle BGC, the straight line GK falls within the angle BGC; hence K lies on the circumference BC between B and C, and the circumference BK is a part of the circumference BC.

**Step 4.** In the equal circles ABC and DEF the angles BGK and EHF at the centres are equal; therefore they stand on equal circumferences, so that the circumference BK is equal to the circumference EF [3.26].

**Step 5.** But the circumference EF is equal to the circumference BC by hypothesis. Therefore the circumference BK is equal to the circumference BC [CN1].

**Step 6.** But BK is a part of BC, so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible, since the whole is greater than the part [CN5]. Therefore the angle BGC is not unequal to the angle EHF; that is, the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF.

**Step 7.** Now the angle BGC at the centre and the angle BAC at the circumference stand on the same circumference BC; therefore the angle BGC is double of the angle BAC [3.20]. Likewise the angle EHF at the centre and the angle EDF at the circumference stand on the same circumference EF; therefore the angle EHF is double of the angle EDF [3.20].

**Step 8.** Since the angle BGC is equal to the angle EHF (Step 6), the double of the angle BAC is equal to the double of the angle EDF. Therefore the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF; for if one of them, say BAC, were the greater, its double BGC would contain the double of EDF, namely EHF, as a part, and so would be greater than EHF [CN5], contrary to Step 6.

**Step 9.** Therefore in equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In equal circles equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less.
result.proof:
**Statement:** In equal circles equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less.

**Step 1.** Let ABC, DEF be equal circles, and in them let AB, DE be equal straight lines, AB cutting off the circumference ACB as greater and AGB as less, and DE cutting off the circumference DFE as greater and DHE as less. We must show that the greater circumference ACB is equal to the greater DFE, and the less circumference AGB is equal to the less DHE.

**Step 2.** Take the centres of the circles ABC, DEF; let them be K and L respectively [3.1].

**Step 3.** Join AK, KB, DL, LE [P1].

**Step 4.** Since K is the centre of circle ABC, the straight lines AK, KB drawn from the centre to the circumference are radii of that circle, and likewise DL, LE are radii of circle DEF [D1.15]. Since the circles ABC, DEF are equal, their radii are equal [D3.1]. Therefore AK is equal to DL and KB is equal to LE.

**Step 5.** Also the base AB is equal to the base DE by hypothesis. Thus in the triangles AKB, DLE the two sides AK, KB are equal to the two sides DL, LE respectively, and the base AB is equal to the base DE; therefore the angle AKB is equal to the angle DLE [1.8].

**Step 6.** Now the angle AKB is at the centre K of circle ABC and stands upon the circumference AGB, while the angle DLE is at the centre L of circle DEF and stands upon the circumference DHE. Since the circles are equal and the angles at the centres are equal, they stand on equal circumferences [3.26]. Therefore the circumference AGB is equal to the circumference DHE.

**Step 7.** The whole circle ABC is equal to the whole circle DEF by hypothesis. From these equal wholes subtract the equal circumferences AGB and DHE; the remaining circumferences ACB and DFE are therefore equal [CN3].

**Step 8.** Hence, in the equal circles ABC, DEF, the equal straight lines AB, DE cut off equal circumferences: the greater circumference ACB is equal to the greater DFE, and the less circumference AGB is equal to the less DHE. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 3.1, P1, D1.15, D3.1, 1.8, 3.26, CN3

result.statement: In equal circles equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC, DEF be equal circles, and in them let equal circumferences BGC, EHF be cut off, so that circumference BGC is equal to circumference EHF. Join the straight lines BC, EF (P1). I say that BC is equal to EF.

**Step 2.** Take the centres of the circles, K of circle ABC and L of circle DEF (3.1), and join BK, KC, EL, LF (P1).

**Step 3.** Since the circumference BGC is equal to the circumference EHF, and the angles BKC, ELF stand at the centres K, L upon these circumferences, the angle BKC is equal to the angle ELF (3.27).

**Step 4.** Since the circles ABC, DEF are equal, their radii are equal (D3.1); therefore BK is equal to EL, and KC is equal to LF.

**Step 5.** Thus in the triangles BKC, ELF the two sides BK, KC are equal to the two sides EL, LF respectively, and the angle BKC contained by them is equal to the angle ELF; therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF (1.4).

**Step 6.** Therefore in equal circles equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To bisect a given circumference.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ADB be the given circumference of a circle, with extremities A and B; it is required to bisect it. Join the straight line AB [P1].

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at the point C [1.10], so that AC = CB.

**Step 3.** From the point C draw CD at right angles to AB [1.11], and let D be the point where this perpendicular meets the given circumference ADB. Join AD and DB [P1].

**Step 4.** In the triangles ACD and BCD: AC = CB (Step 2), CD is common, and the angle ACD equals the angle BCD, since each is a right angle (Step 3) and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]. Thus the two sides AC, CD are equal to the two sides BC, CD respectively, and the included angles are equal; therefore the base AD is equal to the base DB [1.4].

**Step 5.** Since the straight line CD cuts the straight line AB into two equal parts and at right angles, the centre of the circle lies on CD [3.1, Porism]. Hence DC produced through the centre is terminated by the circumference at a point E, and DE is a diameter of the circle [D1.17], cutting the circumference into two semicircles DAE and DBE [D1.18]. Because C lies between A and B on AB and C lies on DE, the points A and B fall on opposite sides of DE, so A lies on the semicircle DAE and B on the semicircle DBE. The circumference AD is therefore a part of the semicircle DAE, and the circumference DB a part of the semicircle DBE; consequently each of the circumferences AD, DB is less than a semicircle [CN5], i.e., each is the lesser of the two circumferences cut off by its chord.

**Step 6.** Now in a circle equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less [3.28]. Since the straight line AD is equal to the straight line DB (Step 4), and the circumferences AD and DB are both the lesser circumferences cut off by these chords (Step 5), the circumference AD is equal to the circumference DB.

**Step 7.** Therefore the given circumference ADB has been bisected at the point D. Q.E.F.

result.statement: In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, let BC be a diameter of it, and let E be its centre; since BC is a diameter, it passes through the centre E (D1.17). The semicircle BAC is the figure contained by the diameter BC and the circumference BAC cut off by it (D1.18). Take any point A on the circumference BAC and join BA, AC (P1). Then the angle BAC, contained by the straight lines joined from A to the extremities B, C of the diameter, is the angle in the semicircle BAC (D3.8).

**Step 2.** The straight line AC divides the circle into the two segments ABC and ADC, each contained by AC and a circumference (D3.6). Because the diameter BC bisects the circle (D1.17), the circumference ABC consists of the circumference AB together with the semicircle from B to C on the side remote from A; hence the segment ABC is greater than a semicircle (CN5). The circumference ADC is a part of the semicircle BAC; hence the segment ADC is less than a semicircle (CN5). Take any point D on the circumference ADC and join AD, DC (P1). Then ABC is an angle in the greater segment ABC, and ADC is an angle in the less segment ADC (D3.8).

**Step 3.** Join AE (P1), and produce BA beyond A to a point F (P2).

**Step 4.** Since E is the centre, BE = EA and EA = EC (D1.15). In triangle ABE the sides BE, EA are equal, so the angle ABE equals the angle BAE (1.5). In triangle AEC the sides EA, EC are equal, so the angle EAC equals the angle ECA (1.5).

**Step 5.** E lies on BC between B and C, so AE falls within the angle BAC, and the angle BAC is the sum of the angles BAE, EAC; moreover the angle ABE is the angle ABC and the angle ECA is the angle ACB. Adding the two equalities of Step 4 (CN2), the angle BAC equals the sum of the angles ABC, ACB.

**Step 6.** Since the side BA of triangle ABC is produced to F, the angle FAC is an exterior angle of that triangle and equals the sum of the two interior and opposite angles ABC, ACB (1.32). Therefore the angle BAC equals the angle FAC (CN1).

**Step 7.** The straight line CA, set up on the straight line BF, makes the adjacent angles BAC, CAF equal to one another; therefore each of them is right (D1.10). Thus the angle BAC in the semicircle BAC is right. (First part.)

**Step 8.** In triangle ABC the two angles ABC, BAC are together less than two right angles (1.17). The angle BAC is right (Step 7); therefore the angle ABC is less than a right angle. Since all angles in the same segment are equal to one another (3.21), every angle in the greater segment ABC is less than a right angle. (Second part.)

**Step 9.** The points A, B, C, D lie on the circumference, so ABCD is a quadrilateral in the circle, and its opposite angles ABC, ADC are together equal to two right angles (3.22). The angle ABC is less than a right angle (Step 8); therefore the angle ADC is greater than a right angle. Since all angles in the same segment are equal to one another (3.21), every angle in the less segment ADC is greater than a right angle. (Third part.)

**Step 10.** The angle of the greater segment ABC is the angle contained by the straight line AC and the circumference ABC (D3.7). The straight line BA, joining the points B, A of the circumference, falls within the circle (3.2), and so lies within the segment ABC; hence the rectilineal angle BAC is a part of the angle contained by AC and the circumference ABC. The whole is greater than the part (CN5), and the angle BAC is right (Step 7); therefore the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle. (Fourth part.)

**Step 11.** The angle of the less segment ADC is the angle contained by the straight line AC and the circumference ADC (D3.7). Since F lies on BA produced beyond A, F is on the side of AC remote from B, which is the side on which the circumference ADC lies; and the circumference ADC lies on the same side of BF as C. Hence the circumference ADC falls within the angle CAF, and the angle contained by AC and the circumference ADC is a part of the angle CAF. The whole is greater than the part (CN5), and the angle CAF is right (Step 7); therefore the angle of the less segment is less than a right angle. (Fifth part.)

Therefore in a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle. Q.E.D.

Path note: in Step 8 the same inequality follows from 1.32 applied to triangle ABC (three angles together equal to two right angles, one of them right); 1.17 is cited as the more direct statement.

**USED:** P1, P2, CN1, CN2, CN5, D1.10, D1.15, D1.17, D1.18, D3.6, D3.7, D3.8, 1.5, 1.17, 1.32, 3.2, 3.21, 3.22

result.statement: If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact there be drawn across, in the circle, a straight line cutting the circle, the angles which it makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF touch the circle at the point B, and from B let the straight line BD be drawn across in the circle, cutting it, so that its other extremity D lies on the circumference. From B draw BA at right angles to EF [1.11] and produce it [P2] until it meets the circumference again at A. Because EF touches the circle at B and BA is drawn from the point of contact at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle lies on BA [3.19]. Thus BA passes through the centre and is terminated at both ends by the circumference, so BA is a diameter of the circle [D1.17], and each of the two segments cut off by BA is a semicircle [D1.18].

**Step 2.** First suppose that BD does not pass through the centre, so that D is distinct from A and lies on one side of the diameter BA. Name the extremities of the tangent so that F lies on the same side of BA as D and E on the other side; then BD falls within the angle ABF, so that the angle ABF is made up of the angles ABD and DBF. Take a point C at random on the circumference BD remote from A (the arc from B to D not containing A), and join AD, DC, CB [P1]. The angles which BD makes with the tangent are DBF and DBE. The segment alternate to the angle DBF is the segment BAD, and the angle in it is the angle BAD; the segment alternate to the angle DBE is the segment DCB, and the angle in it is the angle DCB [D3.8].

**Step 3.** The angle ADB is an angle in the semicircle on the diameter BA, because D is a point on the circumference of that semicircle and DA, DB are joined from D to the extremities A, B of its base [D1.18, D3.8]. Therefore the angle ADB is right [3.31].

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABD the three angles BAD, ABD, ADB are together equal to two right angles [1.32]. Since the angle ADB is a right angle, subtracting it from the two right angles leaves the angles BAD and ABD together equal to one right angle [CN3].

**Step 5.** The angle ABF is right by the construction of Step 1. Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], the angle ABF is equal to the angles BAD and ABD taken together.

**Step 6.** The angle ABF is made up of the angles ABD and DBF (Step 2). Subtracting the angle ABD from the angle ABF and from the sum of BAD and ABD, the remaining angle DBF is equal to the remaining angle BAD [CN3]. That is, the angle DBF which BD makes with the tangent is equal to the angle BAD in the alternate segment BAD.

**Step 7.** The points A, B, C, D all lie on the circumference, A and C being on opposite sides of BD, so ABCD is a quadrilateral in the circle. Therefore its opposite angles BAD and BCD are together equal to two right angles [3.22].

**Step 8.** The straight line BD stands on the straight line EF at B, so the adjacent angles DBF and DBE are together equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 9.** Hence the angles DBF and DBE taken together are equal to the angles BAD and BCD taken together, each pair being equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 10.** Of these, the angle DBF is equal to the angle BAD (Step 6). Subtracting these equals from the equal sums, the remaining angle DBE is equal to the remaining angle BCD [CN3]. That is, the angle DBE which BD makes with the tangent is equal to the angle DCB in the alternate segment DCB.

**Step 11.** It remains to consider the case in which BD passes through the centre. Then BD is a diameter [D1.17], and the straight line joined from the centre to the point of contact B lies along BD and is perpendicular to the tangent EF [3.18]; hence BD is perpendicular to EF, and each of the angles DBF and DBE is right [D1.10]. The two segments into which BD divides the circle are semicircles [D1.18], and the angle in each of them is right [3.31]. Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], each of the angles DBF and DBE is equal to the angle in the segment alternate to it.

**Step 12.** Therefore, in every case, the angles which the straight line BD drawn from the point of contact makes with the tangent EF are equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
result.proof:
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

Let AB be the given straight line and C the given rectilineal angle. It is required to describe on AB a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to C. The angle C is either acute, right, or obtuse; the three cases are treated in turn.

**Case I: the angle C is acute.**

**Step 1.** On the straight line AB and at the point A on it, construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23].

**Step 2.** From the point A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the angle BAD (being equal to the acute angle C) is less than the right angle DAK, and AB, AK lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AB falls within the angle DAK; hence the angle BAK is the excess of the right angle DAK over the angle BAD, and so the angle BAK is less than a right angle.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11], taking FG on the same side of AB as K.

**Step 4.** The straight line AB falls on the two straight lines AK and FG and makes with them the interior angles BAK and AFG on the same side; the angle BAK is less than a right angle (Step 2) and the angle AFG is right (Step 3), so together they are less than two right angles. Therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at the point G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 5.** Since AF is equal to FB (Step 3) and FG is common, the two sides AF, FG are equal to the two sides BF, FG respectively; and the angle AFG is equal to the angle BFG, both being right angles [P4]. Therefore the base AG is equal to the base BG [1.4].

**Step 6.** With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]. Since GB is equal to GA (Step 5), the point B lies on the circumference of this circle [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] until it meets the circumference again at the point E; then AE, passing through the centre G and terminated in both directions by the circumference, is a diameter of the circle [D1.17]. The figure contained by the straight line AB and the circumference AEB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6].

**Step 7.** The straight line AD was drawn from A at right angles to AK (Step 2), and the diameter AE lies along AK; thus AD is drawn from the extremity A of the diameter AE at right angles to that diameter. Therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 8.** Since AB falls within the angle DAK (Step 2), the ray AK, and hence the point E on it, lies on the opposite side of AB from D; so the segment AEB is the segment alternate to the angle DAB. Now AD touches the circle at A, and from the point of contact A the straight line AB has been drawn across in the circle, cutting it; therefore the angle DAB, which AB makes with the tangent AD, is equal to the angle in the alternate segment AEB, that is, to the angle AEB [3.32], which is the angle in the segment AEB [D3.8].

**Step 9.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 1); therefore the angle AEB is also equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on the given straight line AB the segment AEB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case II: the angle C is right.**

**Step 10.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and with centre F and distance FA describe a circle [P3]. Since FB is equal to FA, the point B lies on the circumference [D1.15]. Thus AB passes through the centre F and is terminated in both directions by the circumference, so AB is a diameter [D1.17], and the figure contained by AB and the circumference cut off by it on either side is a semicircle [D1.18]; let E be any point on this circumference, and join AE, EB [P1].

**Step 11.** The angle AEB, being the angle in the semicircle AEB, is a right angle [3.31]. But the angle C is also a right angle, and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]; therefore the angle AEB is equal to the angle C. Hence on AB the semicircle AEB has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case III: the angle C is obtuse.**

**Step 12.** On AB at the point A construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23], and from A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the right angle DAK is less than the obtuse angle DAB, and AK, AB lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AK falls within the angle DAB; hence the angle KAB is the excess of the angle DAB over the right angle DAK. Since the angle DAB, being a rectilineal angle, is less than two right angles, the angle KAB is less than a right angle.

**Step 13.** Bisect AB at F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11] on the same side of AB as K. The straight line AB falls on AK and FG and makes the interior angles KAB (less than a right angle) and AFG (right) on the same side, together less than two right angles; therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 14.** As in Step 5, AF is equal to FB, FG is common, and the right angles AFG, BFG are equal [P4]; therefore AG is equal to BG [1.4]. With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]; since GB is equal to GA, B lies on its circumference [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] to meet the circumference at E; then AE is a diameter [D1.17], lying along AK, and AD is drawn from its extremity A at right angles to it; therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 15.** In this case AK falls within the angle DAB (Step 12), so K, and with it G and E, lie on the same side of AB as D; the segment alternate to the angle DAB is therefore the segment on the other side of AB. Let H be any point on the circumference on that other side of AB, and join AH, HB [P1]; then AHB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6] and the angle AHB is the angle in it [D3.8]. Since AD touches the circle at A and AB is drawn across in the circle from the point of contact, the angle DAB is equal to the angle AHB in the alternate segment AHB [3.32].

**Step 16.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 12); therefore the angle AHB is equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on AB the segment AHB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AHB equal to the given angle C.

**Step 17.** Therefore in every case, on the given straight line AB a segment of a circle has been described admitting an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle C. Q.E.F.

*Path note:* in Case II the most direct route is taken: the semicircle on AB is described at once and its angle is shown right by 3.31, so neither the construction of the angle BAD nor the tangent AD is needed there; the tangent-and-alternate-segment argument (3.16 Por., 3.32) is used only in the acute and obtuse cases, where it is indispensable.

result.statement: From a given circle to cut off a segment admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle and D the given rectilineal angle. It is required to cut off from the circle ABC a segment admitting an angle equal to the angle D.

**Step 2.** Let a straight line EF be drawn touching the circle ABC, and let B be the point of contact, so that EF touches the circle ABC at the point B [3.17].

**Step 3.** On the straight line FB, and at the point B on it, construct the angle FBC equal to the given angle D [1.23], the side BC being drawn on that side of EF on which the circle ABC lies.

**Step 4.** Since EF touches the circle ABC at B, no straight line can be interposed into the space between EF and the circumference of the circle [3.16]. Hence BC, being a straight line through B distinct from EF and lying on the side of the circle, falls within the circle; therefore, being produced, it meets the circumference again. Let C be the point at which it meets the circumference. Thus BC has been drawn across in the circle from the point of contact B and cuts the circle, and it cuts off from the circle the segment BAC lying on the opposite side of BC from F.

**Step 5.** Since the straight line EF touches the circle ABC at B, and from the point of contact B the straight line BC has been drawn across in the circle cutting it, the angle FBC which BC makes with the tangent is equal to the angle in the alternate segment BAC [3.32]; that is, to the angle BAC contained by the straight lines joined to B and C from any point A taken on the circumference of the segment BAC [D3.8].

**Step 6.** But the angle FBC was constructed equal to the angle D (Step 3). Therefore the angle in the segment BAC is also equal to the angle D [CN1].

**Step 7.** Therefore from the given circle ABC the segment BAC has been cut off admitting an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle D. Q.E.F.

result.statement: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and in it let the two straight lines AC and BD cut one another at the point E. We must show that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Take the centre F of the circle [3.1].

**Step 2.** First, suppose that E is the centre F. Then AE, EC, DE, EB are all drawn from the centre to the circumference, so they are equal to one another [D1.15]. Hence the rectangle AE, EC is the square on AE, the rectangle DE, EB is the square on DE, and since AE = DE these squares are equal. So the two rectangles are equal, and the proposition holds in this case.

**Step 3.** Next, suppose that E is not the centre F. We first establish the following for either of the two given straight lines: if XY is one of them (X, Y being its extremities on the circumference) and E the point on it at which they cut, then the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. Join FX [P1].

**Step 4.** Case (a): XY passes through the centre F. Then FX = FY, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference [D1.15], so XY is bisected at F; and since E is not F, XY is cut into unequal segments at E. Therefore, XY being cut into equal segments at F and into unequal segments at E, the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on FE is equal to the square on the half, that is, on FX [2.5]. This is the required equation.

**Step 5.** Case (b): XY does not pass through F. From F draw FG perpendicular to XY [1.12], so that the angles at G are right [D1.10]. Since FG is a straight line through the centre which cuts the straight line XY, not through the centre, at right angles, it also bisects it [3.3]; therefore XG = GY.

**Step 6.** Suppose E does not coincide with G. Then XY is cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at E; therefore the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GX [2.5]. Add the square on GF to each: the rectangle XE, EY together with the squares on EG, GF is equal to the squares on GX, GF [CN2].

**Step 7.** In the triangle EGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on EG, GF are equal to the square on FE; and in the triangle XGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on GX, GF are equal to the square on FX [1.47]. Hence, from Step 6, the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FX [CN1].

**Step 8.** If instead E coincides with G, then XE = EY, so the rectangle XE, EY is the square on XE; and FE is the perpendicular FG, so in the right-angled triangle XEF the square on XE together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX [1.47]. Thus again the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX.

**Step 9.** Therefore in every case (Steps 4 to 8) the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. Applying this to the straight line AC: the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FA. Applying it to the straight line BD: the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FB.

**Step 10.** But FA = FB, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference [D1.15], so the square on FA is equal to the square on FB. Therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on EF [CN1].

**Step 11.** Subtract the square on EF from each: the rectangle AE, EC is equal to the rectangle DE, EB [CN3].

**Step 12.** Therefore, combining Step 2 with Step 11, in every case the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two straight lines, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference will be equal to the square on the tangent.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let a point D be taken outside the circle ABC, and from D let the two straight lines DCA, DB fall on the circle; let DCA cut the circle (meeting the convex circumference first at C and the concave circumference at A) and let DB touch it at B. I say that the rectangle contained by AD, DC is equal to the square on DB. Two cases arise: DCA either passes through the centre or it does not.

**Step 2.** Case 1: let DCA pass through the centre, and let F be the centre of the circle ABC. Join FB (P1).

**Step 3.** Since DB touches the circle at B and FB is joined from the centre to the point of contact, FB is perpendicular to DB; therefore the angle FBD is right (3.18).

**Step 4.** Since F is the centre, FA is equal to FC (D1.15); hence the straight line AC is bisected at F, and the straight line CD is added to it in a straight line.

**Step 5.** Therefore the rectangle contained by AD, DC together with the square on FC is equal to the square on FD (2.6).

**Step 6.** But FC is equal to FB (D1.15); therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on FB is equal to the square on FD.

**Step 7.** Since the angle FBD is right, the square on FD is equal to the squares on FB, BD (1.47).

**Step 8.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on FB is equal to the squares on FB, BD (CN1).

**Step 9.** Let the square on FB be subtracted from each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC which remains is equal to the square on the tangent DB (CN3).

**Step 10.** Case 2: let DCA not pass through the centre of the circle ABC. Let the centre E be taken (3.1), and from E let EF be drawn perpendicular to AC (1.12); join EB, EC, ED (P1). Since D lies on the straight line AC produced, F, C, D lie in one straight line, and the angles EFC, EFD are right.

**Step 11.** Since DB touches the circle at B and EB is joined from the centre to the point of contact, the angle EBD is right (3.18).

**Step 12.** Since the straight line EF through the centre cuts the straight line AC not through the centre at right angles, it also bisects it; therefore AF is equal to FC (3.3).

**Step 13.** Since the straight line AC is bisected at F and CD is added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by AD, DC together with the square on FC is equal to the square on FD (2.6).

**Step 14.** Let the square on FE be added to each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the squares on CF, FE is equal to the squares on FD, FE (CN2).

**Step 15.** Since the angle EFC is right, the squares on CF, FE are equal to the square on CE (1.47); and since the angle EFD is right, the squares on FD, FE are equal to the square on ED (1.47).

**Step 16.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on CE is equal to the square on ED (CN1).

**Step 17.** But CE is equal to EB, since E is the centre (D1.15); therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on EB is equal to the square on ED.

**Step 18.** Since the angle EBD is right, the square on ED is equal to the squares on EB, BD (1.47).

**Step 19.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on EB is equal to the squares on EB, BD (CN1).

**Step 20.** Let the square on EB be subtracted from each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC which remains is equal to the square on the tangent DB (CN3).

**Step 21.** Therefore in either case, if a point be taken outside a circle and from it two straight lines fall on the circle, one cutting it and the other touching it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the cutting line and the part intercepted outside between the point and the convex circumference is equal to the square on the tangent. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which falls on it will touch the circle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let D be a point taken outside the circle ABC, and from D let the two straight lines DCA and DB fall on the circle; let DCA cut the circle (meeting the circumference at C and at A), and let DB fall on the circle at B; and let the rectangle contained by AD, DC be equal to the square on DB. I say that DB touches the circle ABC.

**Step 2.** From the point D draw the straight line DE touching the circle ABC [3.17]; let F be the centre of the circle ABC [3.1]; and join FE, FB, FD [P1].

**Step 3.** Since DE touches the circle ABC and FE is joined from the centre F to the point of contact E, FE is perpendicular to DE; therefore the angle FED is right [3.18].

**Step 4.** Since DE touches the circle ABC and DCA cuts it, the rectangle contained by AD, DC is equal to the square on DE [3.36].

**Step 5.** But the rectangle contained by AD, DC is also equal to the square on DB, by hypothesis. Therefore the square on DE is equal to the square on DB [CN1]; hence the straight line DE is equal to the straight line DB.

**Step 6.** Moreover FE is equal to FB, since both are drawn from the centre F to the circumference of the circle [D1.15].
